taxonomyNote: Animal Diversity Web lists cowlesi only as a subspecies of Sceloporus undulatus; NatureServe and the Arizona field guide treat it as a full species.
fieldMarks: Small lizard (to about 76 mm snout-vent), gray-brown to golden-brown with pointed, keeled, overlapping scales and two light stripes on the back.
Males have two large bright-blue belly patches usually edged dark gray or black, and two blue blotches on the throat; belly patches faint or absent in females.
Gravid females often have an orange or yellow tint on the back.
Paired throat blotches separate it from the common sagebrush lizard; lack of side blotches separates it from the side-blotched lizard.
behavior: Diurnal; most active mid-morning and late afternoon in summer and all day in spring and fall.
Sit-and-wait forager that takes the ground but climbs rocks, trees, fence posts and wood piles to bask.
Eats termites, ants, beetles, grasshoppers, flies, spiders, snails and small lizards; females lay eggs from mid-May to mid-August (7-9 eggs in New Mexico).
habitat: Usually open, sunlit areas with basking sites such as rock piles and logs, from Chihuahuan desertscrub and grassland to woodland and montane conifer forest.
range: Southwestern United States: southern and eastern Arizona, New Mexico and western Texas (NatureServe also lists Navajo Nation) into northern Chihuahua; not in Canada.

lookalikes.name: Plateau lizard (striped plateau lizard)
lookalikes.howToTell: Nearly identical in appearance to the southwestern fence lizard but genetically distinct, and its boundary with cowlesi is poorly known; the striped plateau lizard has a plain belly (Reptiles of Arizona).
